extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and practitioners interested in cognitive psychology and therapeutic techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Explaining the concept, mechanisms, therapeutic uses, and distinctions of cognitive reframing—including how humor can facilitate reframing—and examples of when positive/negative/neutral reframes are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of cognitive reframing
rubrics_metrics.description: Cognitive reframing is a psychological technique that consists of identifying and then changing the way situations, experiences, events, ideas and emotions are viewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as the process by which such situations or thoughts are challenged and then changed; framed as a general mental shift that can be applied to many kinds of situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process: identify, challenge, change
rubrics_metrics.description: The reframing process involves identifying a thought or perspective, challenging it, and then changing it to a different frame of reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article emphasizes the procedural nature (identify → challenge → change). This conceptual stepwise framing is the operative technique underlying therapeutic and everyday reframing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive restructuring as therapeutic subset
rubrics_metrics.description: In cognitive therapy, cognitive reframing is referred to as cognitive restructuring — a therapeutic act of consciously changing one's mindset to strengthen oneself with a positive connotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developed from Beck's work with depressed patients; restructuring is typically done under therapist guidance, is conscious, and aims at positive change rather than neutral or negative reframes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from cognitive distortion
rubrics_metrics.description: Cognitive distortions are exaggerated and typically negative thoughts not supported by a rational thought process; they are problems that cognitive reframing/restructuring may address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distortions can lead to depression and poor decisions; where distortions are present, cognitive restructuring may be indicated to correct irrational negative frames.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness criterion (conscious vs. subconscious)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cognitive reframing can occur subconsciously, whereas cognitive restructuring is a conscious, often therapist-guided process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: hindsight bias is an unconscious reframing to retain pride/self-esteem. This distinction matters for intervention choice (self-guided vs. therapeutic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Therapeutic applications and outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Cognitive reframing can be used to improve memory, reduce test anxiety, and help parents and children cope with disabilities, among other therapeutic outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: memory-impaired individuals told their memory could improve by shifting perspective experienced memory improvement after treatment; parents of disabled children benefited from viewing experiences more positively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of positive humor to facilitate reframing
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive humor (as opposed to mean-spirited or negative humor) can facilitate cognitive reframing by shifting emotional responses toward positivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study example: participants exposed to unpleasant pictures were invited to create a positive joke, a negative joke, or no joke; positive jokes elicited positive emotions. Guidance/anti-pattern: favor positivity-based humor for reappraisal rather than mean-spirited humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valence flexibility: positive, negative, and neutral reframes
rubrics_metrics.description: Reframing can produce positive, negative, or neutral (objective) shifts in perspective; restructuring specifically emphasizes positive shifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative reframing can be intentionally used (e.g., actors inducing sadness), and neutral reframing can be used to make viewpoints more objective and less polarized. Choice of valence depends on the goal (emotion regulation, performance, objectivity).
